title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Sofia Martinez
body:
Summary

This page consolidates Redwood's cross-cutting architecture and standards: API, coding, infrastructure (IaC), model-serving, observability, performance targets, and the ADR process. The goal is a single authoritative reference teams use when designing, reviewing, and operating services that integrate with Redwood inference runtime and control plane.

Scope
- Applies to all services in the inference product surface (hosted API, dedicated, and private): runtime-inference, routing-service, model-registry, control-plane, console-backend, and integrations.
- Excludes ephemeral experiments: prototypes living in personal repos must be promoted through PRs and a small design review before productionization.

1) API Standards
- API design style: RESTful JSON-over-HTTPS for control-plane APIs; gRPC recommended for internal high-throughput RPCs between runtime components. Public client-facing inference API follows OpenAPI v3.1.
- Endpoint naming: use nouns, plural resources (e.g., POST /v1/models, GET /v1/models/{model_id}/versions). Version in path (v1); support header-version for gradual migrations (Accept-Version).
- Request/response schema: always include schema.version and request_id top-level fields. All responses must include error metadata with machine-readable error.code and human_message.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination for heavy lists (limit + cursor). Avoid offset pagination for model and job lists.
- Rate limiting and quotas: 429 with Retry-After header. Per-tenant and per-route quotas enforced by routing-service and rate-limiter sidecar. Document usage in API reference.
- Idempotency: POST endpoints that create resources must accept Idempotency-Key header.
- Authentication: JWT bearer tokens for hosted API; mTLS for internal service-to-service where required; OAuth2 for third-party integrations.
- Backwards compatibility: additive schema changes only; breaking changes require deprecation policy and ADR.

2) Coding Standards (opinionated)
- Languages: Go for infra/runtime services, Python/TypeScript for SDKs and tooling. Exceptions allowed with approval.
- Formatting & linting: gofmt/golangci-lint for Go; Black + Flake8 for Python; ESLint + Prettier for TypeScript. CI must fail on lint/format violations.
- Tests: unit tests with >= 90% coverage for critical runtime logic; integration tests for API contracts. Use deterministic seeds for stochastic tests.
- PR guidance: max 400 lines changed without design review; include a short summary, rollout plan, and potential backward-incompatibilities. Use conventional commits for automated changelogs.
- Secrets handling: no secrets in code or repo. Use secrets-manager with explicit IAM roles.

3) Infra & IaC Standards
- IaC tooling: Terraform (primary) for cloud infra; Terragrunt patterns allowed. Modules must be published to the internal registry.
- Naming & tags: all cloud resources must include tags: team, service, env, cost_center. Resource names follow: rdw-{team}-{service}-{env}-{short}.
- Networking: VPC-per-environment; private subnets for runtime-inference; public ALBs only for ingress endpoints. Use shared transit gateways for private deployments when required.
- Secrets & KMS: use cloud KMS (or customer KMS for Private) with key rotation every 365 days. HSM integration required for FIPS-sensitive customers.
- Deploys: blue/green or canary deployments by default for control-plane and runtime-inference. Terraform changes require plan & apply in CI with PR approval.

4) Model-Serving Standards
- Model metadata: every model must have a model card in model-registry containing architecture, tokenizer, max_seq_length, quantization_profile, license, and owner. Schema versioned.
- Versioning: semantic-like model versions (e.g., 1.2.0-20260215) and immutable model artifacts. Support aliases (stable, canary).
- Quantization profiles: define named profiles (fp16, int8-q4_0, int8-q4_1) with expected throughput/latency tradeoffs and quality delta. Profiles stored alongside model card.
- Fallback policy: routing-service should define fallback chains for each route: primary model -> compatible smaller model -> cached-response fallback. Document capacity tiers and compatibility matrix.
- KV cache and prefix caching: runtime-inference must expose cache hit/miss metrics and a cache-control header on responses when appropriate.
- Safety & guardrails: implement per-tenant content filters and use quality-guardrails harness before rolling models to production.

5) Observability Standards
- Metrics: use Prometheus exposition for runtime metrics. Standard metric names and labels: request_latency_seconds{route,model,tenant,code}, request_size_bytes, tokens_generated_total, kv_cache_hit_ratio{model}.
- SLOs and targets (see Performance below). Export p50/p95/p99 latency histograms.
- Tracing: distributed traces with W3C tracecontext. Services must propagate traceparent and include spans for routing, model-eval, decode.
- Logs: structured JSON logs (timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, tenant_id, message). Log retention: 90 days for production by default; option for extended retention as add-on.
- Alerts & runbooks: alerts map to runbooks in eng-sre/runbooks. All alerts must have a documented owner and runbook link.

6) Performance Standards & SLOs
- Availability SLOs: 99.9% uptime for hosted API and control-plane services; 99.5% for non-critical background services.
- Latency SLOs (examples):
  | Route Class | Payload | p50 < | p95 < | p99 < |
  |-------------|---------|-------:|------:|------:|
  | interactive-text-generation | 128 tokens | 50 ms | 150 ms | 500 ms |
  | standard-text-generation | 512 tokens | 100 ms | 300 ms | 900 ms |
  | embeddings | 1k tokens | 30 ms | 120 ms | 400 ms |
- Error budget: 0.1% monthly for critical routes. Exceeding error budget triggers reliability initiative and freeze on non-essential launches.
- Autoscaling & batching: runtime-inference must support adaptive batching; target batch size tuned per model (documented in quantization_profile). Prefer latency-first configs for interactive routes; throughput-first for batch jobs.
- Resource allocation: GPU selection guidance (A10G for cost-efficiency, A100 for high-throughput) in gpu-fleet-and-capacity. Kernels selected automatically but teams must provide perf profiles when onboarding new architectures.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process
- Template: title, status, context, decision, consequences, alternatives considered, date, authors, reviewers. Save ADRs under /confluence/architecture-and-standards/adrs or in repo docs/adrs with link back to Confluence.
- When to write an ADR: any decision with system-wide impact (breaking API changes, core infra patterns, runtime scheduling, model-card schema changes).
- Review & lifecycle: draft -> in_review (stakeholders listed) -> published. Major ADRs require a 1-week review window and SRE/product approval. Deprecation ADRs must include migration plan and timeline (>= 90 days for API breaking changes).
- Example ADRs (existing):
  - ADR-2025-07: routing-service-fallback-policy (decision: prioritized model fallbacks per tenant).
  - ADR-2025-11: model-card-schema-v2 (decision: add quantization_profile and quality_delta fields).
  - ADR-2026-01: runtime-batching-strategy (decision: hybrid adaptive batching with latency tiers).

8) Review & Ownership
- Document ownership: architecture-and-standards is owned by the Engineering Architecture working group; primary contact: sofia.martinez@redwood.example.com. Team owners for each standard section must be listed in the header of each related doc.
- Review cadence: annual review for core standards; after major incidents or product changes trigger immediate review.

9) Rollout checklist (new service or major change)
1. Create ADR if decision is cross-cutting.
2. Implement API & model-card schema changes behind feature flags.
3. Unit + integration + contract tests; add API schema to OpenAPI and run contract tests.
4. Canary rollout to small percentage of tenants; monitor SLOs for 48 hours.
5. Gradual ramp to 100% with rollback plan and automated rollback on alert conditions.
6. Update runbooks, dashboards, and docs.

Appendix: Quick examples
- Example curl to call inference (hosted):
  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.example.com/v1/generate 
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
    -d '{"model":"gpt-redwood-1", "input":"Translate to French: Hello world", "max_tokens":64, "request_id":"$(uuidgen)"}'

- Terraform module example snippet (naming):
  module "rdw_runtime_cluster" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@internal.repo/terraform-modules.git//rdw-runtime-cluster"
    name   = "rdw-eng-runtime-inference-prod"
    tags = { team = "eng", service = "runtime-inference", env = "prod" }
  }

Conformance & next steps
- All teams should read and confirm conformance within 60 days of this publication. Exceptions require an ADR and an approved risk mitigation plan.
- Roadmap items: create automated linters for API contract enforcement; add model-card validator to onboarding CI; publish standard dashboards and alert rules as code in eng-platform/dashboards.
